distractors.reason: We don't say 'narrow schedule'. 'Narrow' describes width, like a narrow street or a narrow path.
We don't say 'thin schedule'. 'Thin' describes the thickness of objects, like thin paper.
We don't say 'close schedule'. 'Close' means near in distance or relationship, not a full timetable.

example_sentence: I have a ___ schedule this week, so I can't meet you.
l1_interference: Los hispanohablantes a veces traducen 'apretado' como 'strict' o 'narrow' y dicen 'narrow schedule'. Con 'schedule' use siempre 'tight', no 'narrow'.
explanation: 'Tight' describes a schedule with very little free time between appointments or tasks. It is the usual adjective for a full, pressed timetable.

related_collocations.example: My mother has a busy schedule at work.
The teacher has a full schedule today.
She works a flexible schedule, so she can choose her hours.

memory_tip: TIGHT = very little free time in a schedule (tight deadline, tight schedule) | NARROW = width only (narrow street, narrow door)
